items.title: Conceptual Framework for AI Enabled Learning and Sustainable Organizational Development
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to transform organizational learning and strengthen sustainable development. However, existing research often examines AI capability, organizational learning, digital innovation strategy, and sustainability separately. This study aims to develop an integrated conceptual framework explaining how AI-enabled organizational learning may contribute to sustainable organizational development. An integrative literature review was conducted using structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by citation tracking through Google Scholar. Thirty-one scholarly sources were synthesized according to their theoretical constructs, explanatory mechanisms, and levels of analysis. The framework integrates the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capability Theory, Technology-Organization-Environment framework, and technology acceptance theories. The study proposes an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Learning Ecosystem (AILE) framework comprising four direct propositions linking AI Capability, AI-Enabled Learning Ecosystem, Digital Innovation Strategy, and Sustainable Organizational Development. Two additional propositions identify employee engagement and technology acceptance, alongside resource efficiency and AI governance, as moderating conditions. The framework also introduces organizational sustainability indicators, a resource cost-benefit assessment, and a four-stage implementation roadmap. The proposed framework offers a theoretical foundation for examining how AI-supported learning can contribute to organizational resilience, workforce development, and responsible digital innovation. Its potential relevance extends to SDGs 4, 8, and 9. As the framework remains conceptual, longitudinal and multilevel empirical studies are required to validate the proposed relationships and assess their practical effectiveness.

items.title: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications
items.abstract: Abstract Wearable sensors enable continuous acquisition of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals during exercise, providing data to support sports performance assessment, training regulation, fatigue monitoring, and rehabilitation interventions. However, signal reliability and multidimensional data analysis under complex motion conditions remain constrained by device functionality. Conductive composites can improve sensor flexibility, interfacial conformability, and signal acquisition performance, while artificial intelligence (AI) enables movement pattern recognition, state assessment, and outcome prediction from complex data. Their integration is advancing wearable systems toward multimodal sensing and intelligent analysis. Guided by application needs in sports, this review summarizes emerging applications of wearable sensing technologies enabled by conductive composites and AI. First, the relevance to sports science and the data characteristics of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals are introduced. The functional characteristics, representative applications, and major limitations of conductive polymer, carbon-based, MXene, and hydrogel composites are then summarized. Regarding algorithms, the fundamental principles of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) are discussed, with comparisons of their capabilities in feature extraction, temporal modeling, and multisource data analysis, as well as their input data requirements. On this basis, advances in the application of these systems to sports performance and sport-specific movement monitoring, exercise-induced fatigue monitoring and assessment, sports injury identification and evaluation, and intelligent monitoring of sports rehabilitation are reviewed followed by a discussion of current challenges and future directions. Through the coordinated integration of material design, signal acquisition, and intelligent analysis, wearable systems are expected to enable continuous, reliable, and individualized assessment of exercise-related states, with further applications in real-time feedback, risk alerts, and training decision support, providing a technological foundation for scientifically informed training, sports rehabilitation, and individual health management.

items.title: Construction of composite hydrophobic coating with insulation and anti-corrosion functions using non-isocyanate polyurethane and silica aerogel
items.abstract: Thermal insulation and anticorrosion coatings play a critical role in safeguarding industrial equipment and infrastructure. Consequently, the development of high performance, environmentally benign hydrophobic coatings has emerged as a key research priority. Conventional polyurethane coatings rely on toxic isocyanates and petroleum-derived feedstocks, raising significant environmental and occupational health concerns. Moreover, their single-component matrix inherently limits synergistic enhancement of both thermal insulation and anticorrosion performance. To address these challenges, this study reports the design and fabrication of an environmentally friendly non-isocyanate polyurethane (NIPU) composite hydrophobic coating. Specifically, a carbamate diol (CD10) was synthesized via the reaction of bio-sourced decanediamine with propylene carbonate; subsequent modification with itaconic acid yielded the NIPU resin. The raw material propylene carbonate can be synthesized from carbon dioxide, decanediamine is derived from castor oil, and itaconic acid is obtained from citric acid. This resin was then formulated with hydrophobic silica aerogel (SA, 0-4 wt%) and titanium dioxide. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the uniform dispersion of SA within the matrix and revealed a cooperative “physical barrier thermal release” mechanism between SA and TiO 2 , which collectively enhances overall coating functionality. The optimized formulation NIPU/SA-3 (containing 3 wt% SA) demonstrated superior comprehensive performance: a thermal conductivity of 0.0478 W/(m·K) (10.1% lower than that of commercial benchmark coatings), an insulation temperature difference of 18.5°C (59.5% higher), excellent hydrophobicity (water contact angle of 120.12°), robust resistance to corrosion and weak alkaline environments, and favorable mechanical properties. This environmentally friendly composite hydrophobic coating eliminates the need for toxic isocyanates, offering a viable and environmentally benign strategy for developing multifunctional materials with combined anti-corrosion and thermal insulation properties features that hold significant practical potential in construction and industrial applications.

items.title: Contextual prompting and large language models in reflexive thematic analysis: what changes and what remains human
items.abstract: Reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) constructs patterned meaning through researchers’ situated engagement with data, making claims that large language models (LLMs) can perform it conceptually difficult. We examined whether contextual grounding changes model suggestions when methodological guidance is held constant. We compared our human analysis of twelve interviews with Vietnamese university English-language teachers with outputs from two model conditions. Both received identical phase-specific RTA instructions, and only the context-informed condition received a factual briefing on Vietnamese tertiary education. Across three runs per condition, contextual grounding increased the median proportion of labels linked to extracts from 81% to 86% and labels accompanied by rationales from 71% to 79%. It produced more setting-specific suggestions but also unsupported assumptions about hierarchy and face-saving. Neither condition reproduced the situated judgement used to adjudicate competing interpretations. We conclude that model outputs may inform critical reflection but cannot substitute for reflexive interpretation.

items.title: Correctness and Completeness of a Multimodal Large Language Model in the Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations for Proximal Femoral Fractures
items.abstract: Background and Objectives: To compare the diagnostic and therapeutic performance of a multimodal large language model (GPT) with that of two human evaluators in proximal femoral fracture (PFF) assessment, focusing on correctness and completeness. Materials and Methods: A consecutive series of 250 PFFs was reconstructed into standardized clinical scenarios including radiographs and structured clinical data. Each case was independently evaluated by a trauma fellow, a second-year orthopaedic resident, and GPT. Responses were scored for diagnostic and treatment correctness and completeness. Severe treatment errors were predefined as category-changing mismatches, failure to recognize an existing implant, or incorrect laterality. Results: Fully correct diagnoses were achieved in 97.2% of cases by the fellow, 44.8% by the resident, and 14.0% by GPT (p < 0.001). GPT showed lower odds of correct diagnosis compared with the resident (matched OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.14–0.37) and fellow (OR 0.005, 95% CI 0.0001–0.03), with clustering of errors in extracapsular fractures. Diagnostic completeness also differed significantly (p < 0.001), with GPT providing fully complete assessments in 60.4% of the cases (151/250). Fully correct treatment recommendations were provided in 98.8%, 81.2%, and 36.4% of cases, respectively (p < 0.001). Severe treatment errors occurred in 58.8% of GPT outputs versus 2.0% and 0% for the resident and fellow (OR vs. resident 36.5, 95% CI 13.95–135.75). Although treatment completeness was high (93.2%), 58.8% (147/250) of GPT responses were complete but incorrect. Conclusions: GPT demonstrated substantial limitations in both diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning for PFF, with frequent pattern-dependent errors and a high rate of clinically consequential treatment mismatches.

items.title: Cost-Driven Handover and Service Migration in Healthcare 4.0 Networks
items.abstract: Abstract—Healthcare 4.0 (H4.0) leverages sixth-generation (6G) communications, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) to enable real-time healthcare services. Future H4.0 deployments will rely on integrated Terrestrial and Non-Terrestrial Networks (TN-NTNs), where user mobility and frequent handovers can lead to service disruptions, traffic rerouting, xNF migrations, and increased operational costs, thereby undermining stringent QoS requirements of missioncritical applications. To address these challenges, this paper proposes HEAL, a low-complexity and cost-driven joint handover and service migration framework for 6G-H4.0 networks. HEAL jointly optimizes user association, traffic routing, and any-type Network Function (xNF) placement under mobility constraints for healthcare-oriented Service Function Chains (SFCs), in compliance with ITU-R IMT-2030 requirements. The problem is formulated as a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes total operational expenditure (OPEX) while reducing mobility events and satisfying healthcare QoS constraints. Simulation results show that HEAL reduces execution time by approximately 84% compared to the optimal MILP solution. Moreover, it achieves up to 82% lower OPEX than the stateof- the-art benchmark, while maintaining OPEX within approximately 18% of the optimal solution, demonstrating its suitability for scalable and cost-efficient 6G-H4.0 deployments.

items.title: Creativity × Anticipation × Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Abstract: This chapter presents a novel triadic framework—creativity × anticipation × generative artificial intelligence (C×A×G)—as the foundation for future-oriented education in the post-information society. The core argument is that creativity, anticipation, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) mastery are not independent skills but, rather, interdependent cognitive engines whose integration is vital for thriving in a volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) world. Each domain is first analyzed individually: Creativity is addressed through its dynamic definition, leading to the dynamic universal creative process (DUCP), and the DA VINCI process model, highlighting potential originality and effectiveness as key criteria; anticipation is explored as the necessary cognitive function for foresight-informed decision-making, essential for resilient action under deep uncertainty; and GenAI is presented as a disruptive cognitive augmentation tool with unprecedented influence on ideation, simulation, and implementation processes. Bilateral interactions among these domains are then discussed. The highest potential is the promise of the final synthesis, presented here as the triadic C×A×G framework: a new cognitive ecology for education, in which each ingredient resonates with the others, in a synergy that has a potential way beyond the mere juxtaposition of the separate abilities. The chapter concludes that embedding C×A×G literacy into education would be not only beneficial but also essential for fostering human dignity, autonomy, and adaptive capacity in the face of the accelerating technological transformation. This interdisciplinary effort calls for the creation of transdisciplinary pedagogical infrastructures and the cultivation of a generative epistemology, fit for an age of systemic discontinuity.

items.title: Cross-Cultural Collaboration and Student Learning in an International Community Engagement Program
items.abstract: Although international community engagement programs are widely implemented across higher education, qualitative evidence detailing how students internally process cross-cultural friction and contextual design adaptation remains sparse compared to administrative reporting. This study addresses this gap through a reflection-centered qualitative inquiry, analyzing reflection transcripts from ten Indonesian and Singaporean student participants (BINUS University and Singapore Polytechnic) engaged in short-term rural field projects at A Green and Yayasan KDM. Using reflexive thematic analysis grounded in Kolb's experiential learning cycle and Schön's reflection-in-action, the analysis revealed four core experiential dynamics. Intercultural dialogue developed by combining emotional translation with rapid visual sketching, while working-pace mismatches between structured planning and local flexibility were resolved through nightly debriefings and user-evidence affinity synthesis. Unscripted rural constraints forced a design pivot toward low-tech cardboard mockups refined through elder ergonomic feedback, while an immersive community stay shifted student perspectives away from top-down technical assumptions toward active community listening and empathy-rooted design ethics. These findings offer a reflective framework for structuring debriefings and ethical co-design in international service-learning, moving beyond superficial activity metrics.

items.title: Cue production and evaluative uptake: prompt framing and user judgments in AI-Mediated health communication
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly embedded in everyday information and support-seeking practices, including health-related interactions in which users seek advice, reassurance, or emotional acknowledgment. Yet less is known about how users’ own communicative framing shapes what AI systems produce, and whether such AI-generated emotional and supportive cues are subsequently taken up in users’ evaluations of the interaction. Drawing on research on human-like social cues and cue-based credibility processing, this study distinguishes between cue production and cue uptake in AI-mediated communication. Using a randomized, naturalistic prompt-based experiment, participants engaged in a brief two-turn exchange with ChatGPT using one of three prompt exemplars about sleep difficulty that varied in solution orientation, distress expression, and help-seeking structure. The study combined experimental manipulation, computational analysis of AI-generated responses, and pre–post measures of perceived emotional understanding, credibility, trust, and intended future use. Prompt framing shaped the emotional and supportive cues of AI responses: distress-expressive prompts elicited higher anxiety-related language scores, solution-oriented prompts produced more positive emotional tone, and mixed help-seeking prompts elicited more reassuring language. However, variation in these features was not reliably associated with differential pre–post changes in users’ evaluations. Across conditions, users reported modest increases in perceived emotional understanding, credibility, and intended future use after the interaction. The findings suggest that conversational AI can adapt its language to users’ framing, but such cue production does not necessarily lead to credibility uptake. The study contributes to research on AI-mediated communication by examining emotional cueing in a live, ecologically realistic interaction context.

items.title: Cultivating Creativity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Abstract: This chapter explores how schools can cultivate creativity as a core educational purpose in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on contemporary learning sciences, educational theory, and international case studies, it argues that creativity must be reconceptualized not merely as a skill or disposition but as a systemic outcome requiring structural transformation. The chapter proposes a framework built around three interdependent pillars: personalizable learning pathways that honor learner agency and variability, a pedagogy rooted in problem-finding and interdisciplinary inquiry, and an ethic of human interdependence that prepares students for meaningful global engagement. Through the case study of Chongqing No. 8 School in China and comparative models from Finland, the United States, and the Netherlands, the chapter illustrates how “school within a school” approaches can serve as incubators for educational transformation. It concludes that in order for AI to serve as a catalyst rather than a constraint, schools must embrace ecological innovation; empower educators as co-designers; and reimagine learning as a creative, co-evolutionary human endeavor.

items.title: Culturally Responsive AI-Supported Cancer Pain Education: A Human-Centered Framework for Multilingual Oncology Care
items.abstract: Cancer pain education aims to help patients understand pain, communicate symptoms, and follow clinician-approved management plans; however, improved knowledge does not consistently translate into reduced pain intensity. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for patient-facing education, while evidence supporting culturally and linguistically responsive oncology applications remains limited. This critical perspective develops a human-centered framework for AI-supported cancer pain education in multilingual oncology care. A focused, non-systematic critical synthesis integrated research on cancer pain education, health literacy, cultural adaptation, multilingual communication, and AI governance. No primary data were collected. The framework proposes six interdependent design domains: patient-led co-design and cultural humility; multilingual, accessible, dialogic learning; accurate pain science that avoids reductionist explanations; clearly bounded, evidence-grounded AI functions; explicit human oversight and escalation procedures; and lifecycle governance with equity-focused evaluation. These domains constitute conceptual recommendations requiring empirical evaluation. A staged evaluation pathway progresses from co-design and cognitive testing to offline AI benchmarking, supervised usability pilots, and comparative implementation studies. Initial evaluations should prioritize comprehension, communication, trust, safety, and access across language groups. Potential effects on pain interference and other clinical outcomes remain hypotheses for prospective testing. Illustrative examples involving Moroccan Darija highlight linguistic and cultural adaptation challenges without establishing cancer-specific validation. The proposed AI role is restricted to educational support and does not encompass diagnosis, prescribing, psychotherapy, professional interpretation, or replacement of oncology professionals. By connecting health education, cultural responsiveness, pain science, and responsible AI governance, the framework provides a basis for developing and evaluating multilingual educational support. Its contribution lies in specifying design and evaluation priorities while retaining clinical effectiveness as an open empirical question.

items.title: Current Trends in Augmented Reality in Endoscopic Spine Surgery: A Systematic Review With Real-World Clinical Insights
items.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate current trends, clinical applications, and limitations of augmented reality (AR) in endoscopic spine surgery (ESS). A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses) 2020 guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar were searched for studies published between January 1, 2019, and April 1, 2026. Studies investigating AR, mixed reality, virtual reality, and related immersive technologies in ESS were included. Experimental, preclinical, and clinical studies were considered because of the emerging nature of the field and the limited availability of comparative clinical evidence, whereas case reports and nonrelevant studies were excluded. Eligible studies were categorized as experimental, preclinical, or clinical. Outcomes included operative efficiency, radiation exposure, visualization, ergonomics, cognitive workload, and patient-reported outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions) tool. Six studies were included, comprising 1 experimental training study, 2 preclinical studies, and 3 clinical studies, all involving lumbar procedures. AR-assisted systems consistently improved procedural efficiency, including reductions in puncture attempts, operative time, and radiation exposure. Visualization and workflow were enhanced through improved magnification, an expanded field of view, and integrated imaging. Clinical studies demonstrated reduced surgeon workload and improved ergonomic posture. However, patient-reported outcomes, including pain and disability scores, improved similarly in both AR-assisted and conventional groups, with no significant between-group differences. No study demonstrated validated improvements in surgical accuracy. The overall risk of bias ranged from moderate to serious. Current preliminary evidence suggests that AR-assisted ESS is feasible and may improve visualization, workflow efficiency, radiation exposure, and surgeon ergonomics. However, evidence supporting improvements in surgical accuracy and patient-reported outcomes remains limited. Further high-quality prospective studies are needed to better define the clinical role of immersive technologies in ESS.

items.abstract: This research is systematic literature review aimed at knowing the impact of use generative artificial intelligence on enhancing the mathematical problem-solving abilities of students. Information search via Google Scholar (using the "Publish or Perish" tool) covering the period 2021 to 2026, with reporting conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Thought the selection process 15 articles were obtained to be analyzed. In mathematics learning the use of ChatGPT is most often used in solving problems. The use of Generative AI enhances students’ skills in solving mathematical problems; however, its effectiveness is influenced by the students' existing mathematical proficiency. Although the benefits depend on students’ mathematical abilities, the use of generative AI generally leads to an improvement in students’ problem-solving skills. While Generative AI serves as a learning support tool, teachers retain a crucial role in providing guidance and facilitating exploration. A key challenge identified is the risk of over-reliance on Generative AI.

items.title: Data and AI Literacy in Geography Education: A Needs Assessment of Pre-Service Geography Teachers
items.abstract: The growing importance of data and the ongoing developments in artificial intelligence (AI) necessitate data and AI literacy in various domains. In geography education, successful integration of data and AI requires geography teachers to exhibit competencies. These have been outlined by various frameworks and models, such as TPACK, DPACK, and AI-PACK. However, despite the existence of such frameworks and the recognition that data and AI are relevant to geography education, research with a focus on pre-service geography teachers remains limited, despite its importance to geography education and its ability to provide insights into teacher education by pre-service teachers. This study investigates perceived data- and AI-related needs of pre-service geography teachers who are still in teacher education training but who have gained practical experience in planning and teaching geography lessons. Eighteen pre-service geography teachers from Germany were subjected to semi-structured interviews. The interview transcripts were analyzed using qualitative content analysis (QCA) involving a deductive-inductive approach. The results show that the participants perceive a need for specific competencies in the context of data (e.g., needs for teacher education, such as data literacy) and AI (content-related AI knowledge). Our findings strongly emphasize the importance of integrating data and AI into geography teacher education.

items.title: Data and code for: Label provenance in published artificial intelligence for tax and customs administration: a systematic review
items.abstract: Data, decisions and code behind the systematic review "Label provenance in published artificial intelligence for tax and customs administration: a systematic review" (Sushanta Paul, National Board of Revenue, Bangladesh). The review audits how published evaluations of AI in tax and customs administration obtained their ground-truth labels, how the labelled cases were selected, and whether the headline claims are supported by that evidence. The primary analysis covers 196 studies: 91 from the first search phase and 105 added by a later search. AI involvement. The first coding of every study was done by Claude. Every later step that the OSF registration (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/2ANXY) assigned to humans was done by a panel of five language models from five vendors (openai/gpt-6-astra, google/gemini-4-argon, x-ai/grok-4.7, deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-0813, qwen/qwen3.8-max-0902) under rules written before each run: title-and-abstract screening, the full-text eligibility check, blind adjudication of disputed codes, the second coder and the resolution of second-coder disagreements. No human took part in those steps, so the agreement figures for the main coding are agreement between language models. (Version 1.1.0 adds the one human check, the author's blind re-coding of 25 studies.) The protocol and its two addenda are in work/. Contents: search and screening records and decisions; eligibility decisions with quoted evidence; coding data with verbatim quotes and page numbers; the codebooks; screening sheets, model proposals and keys; the AI-completion protocol and addenda; adjudication, second-coder and resolution inputs and results; the panel's votes, parsed answers, run logs and manifests (prompt hashes, model identifiers, settings); analysis scripts, output tables and figures. README.md lists every folder and how to rerun the analysis. Not included: the full texts of the studies and the text extracted from them (copyright; each study is identified by DOI in the paper's supplementary material and in work/); the raw API response files, which stay with the author (the parsed answers, run logs and manifests are included); API keys. The files are in one zip archive; README.md lists the contents and how to rerun the analysis. Licences: data, documentation and figures CC BY 4.0; code MIT.

items.abstract: This study is a narrative literature review aimed at analyzing the available evidence on the relationship between mental health, academic motivation, and academic performance among dental students, with emphasis on the preclinical-to-clinical transition. A bibliographic search was conducted in scientific databases, selecting studies related to stress, anxiety, depression, motivation, and academic performance in dental education.The results reveal a high prevalence of anxiety and depression, with direct repercussions on academic performance. The clinical transition emerges as the point of greatest psychological vulnerability, marked by the gap between theoretical training and the demands of working with patients. Intrinsic motivation acts as a protective factor, while extrinsic motivation is associated with greater emotional vulnerability.It is concluded that this transition represents a critical stage that requires institutional strategies aimed at promoting psychological well-being and autonomous motivation.

This Review evaluates how generative AI, graph neural networks, molecular language and diffusion models, structure-based design, and multimodal learning can exploit SCLC dependencies for small-molecule discovery. It integrates biomarker-guided patient stratification, resistance, combination therapy, medicinal chemistry, pharmacology, safety, manufacturing, and clinical translation, emphasizing benchmarked, uncertainty-aware, prospectively validated design–build–test–learn workflows.

items.title: Decoding the Unsaid: Social Opacity, Autism, and AI as Accessibility Infrastructure
items.abstract: This conceptual article proposes an environmental framework for understanding social difficulty in autistic adulthood, one that complements rather than replaces existing cognitive accounts. Many autistic adults face employment instability, health care avoidance, relationship rupture, and chronic burnout; predominant frameworks have located these difficulties within the individual in cognitive or communicative differences understood to reduce social success. I argue that a meaningful portion of this difficulty may instead arise from environments that depend structurally on hidden, unstated norms—a condition I term social opacity. I introduce the norm accessibility gap, decomposed into two independently variable environmental dimensions—norm implicitness and explicit scaffolding—in a way that identifies concrete targets for intervention. Drawing on the social model of disability, the double empathy problem, and neurodiversity scholarship, I argue that social difficulty is in part relational and ecological. Against this backdrop, I propose that Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems may eventually function as social accessibility infrastructure—carefully distinguished from individual assistive tools, with significant implications for institutional responsibility and policy. I distinguish two operational modes (interpretive and mediating) corresponding to the two dimensions of the norm accessibility gap and organize applications across a three-stage developmental pathway from individual tools toward institutional infrastructure. The goal of such tools is not normative imitation but increased autonomy, reduced cognitive burden, and reciprocal understanding—not making autistic adults more neurotypical, but making their social environments more accessible. I attend to ethical risks and propose a participatory research agenda led by autistic adults across diverse support profiles. Community Brief This section summarizes the article in plain English for autistic adults, families, clinicians, advocates, and community readers. This article is conceptual—it does not report a clinical trial or empirical study. What is this article about? This article looks at why social life can be so difficult to navigate for many autistic adults—and asks whether AI technology could eventually help. Rather than focusing on what autistic people might find challenging, it examines the social environment itself. Many social settings depend on unwritten, unstated rules that nobody explains. The article calls this social opacity. It introduces a new concept—the norm accessibility gap—to describe how much of a given setting’s social rules are hidden and unexplained, and asks whether AI tools could help reduce this gap. Why is this topic important? Autistic adults face real and serious consequences when social environments rely on hidden norms: job loss, health care avoidance, relationship difficulties, and exhaustion. Most research has focused on helping autistic people adapt to these environments. This article argues that approach places the entire burden on autistic adults—and that environments themselves could be designed more accessibly. This shift from a deficit lens to an environmental one reflects values central to the neurodiversity movement and the social model of disability. What are the key messages? Three ideas are central. First, social environments vary in how opaque they are—some make their expectations clear, others do not. Second, AI systems could potentially support accessibility in two ways: helping autistic adults interpret ambiguous social situations (an interpretive mode) or introducing explicit communication structure that benefits everyone involved (a mediating mode). Third, responsibility for social accessibility should rest with institutions, not solely with autistic adults. The article frames AI as potential infrastructure—like captioning—rather than just an individual assistive tool and describes a pathway in which near-term individual tools help build toward long-term institutional change. How could this help autistic adults? If these ideas are developed responsibly, autistic adults might eventually have better support navigating workplace communication, health care appointments, or situations where unwritten rules feel inaccessible. The goal is not to make autistic adults appear more neurotypical. It is to reduce unnecessary informational barriers in environments that could be made more transparent for everyone. What should happen next? This article is conceptual—it does not report data or test any intervention. The essential next step is participatory research led by autistic adults, including those with diverse communication styles and support needs. Autistic coresearchers should determine which questions matter, whether tools like these would actually be useful, and whether the framework accurately reflects autistic experience. No tool based on these ideas should be developed without that genuine co-leadership.

items.title: Deep gradient explainable framework with ensemble adaptive multi-scale feature fusion for plant disease detection
items.abstract: Accurate detection of crop disease is essential to improve crop productivity and produce healthy products. Convolution based approach has proven excellent accuracy for plant disease detection. Existing methods depend on backbone architecture and lack interpretability, limiting their robustness and practical applicability. Capturing both fine-grained texture patterns and multi-scale contextual information is a challenging task for visually similar disease classes. To address these challenges, proposed study introduces novel deep ensemble learning framework that integrates residual and multi-scale feature extraction with explainable artificial intelligence. Features extracted with a deep hierarchical and multi-scale learning network are fused using an adaptive attention-based feature-level fusion strategy. Based on fused features, the proposed Deep Gradient eXplainer (DGX) generates proper visual explanations and disease-relevant regions. The proposed framework is evaluated on benchmark PlantVillage and custom plant disease datasets and achieves a classification accuracy of 99.31%. Extensive analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed feature fusion technique with DGX. This improves classification accuracy with interpretability. The proposed DGX validates that the model focuses on biologically meaningful regions, which helps to identify the correct disease.

items.title: Deep Learning Techniques for the Creation of Deepfakes
items.abstract: Deepfakes are a product of rapid advances in artificial intelligence. This chapter traverses the deep learning techniques used to create them. For readers new to the subject, it surveys the building blocks of synthetic media generation and the research that established them, and it points to representative software and services. Since the first edition, the toolkit has broadened considerably. Autoencoders and generative adversarial networks, which dominated early deepfake creation, have been joined and, in many tasks, surpassed by diffusion models, while related advances have made convincing voice cloning possible from a few seconds of audio and have extended synthetic generation from images to full text-to-video models. This chapter explains each of these technique families in turn, summarizes the relevant literature, and notes the practical constraints, namely, the data, computing power, and training time that still shape what can be produced. The objective is to give a clear and current account of how deepfakes are made, as a foundation for the discussion of detection that follows.

items.title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
items.abstract: Policymakers and firms have become increasingly dependent on academic research for upstream scientific progress, especially in domains where technical challenges in downstream invention generate demand for additional research. This study examines which academic scientists produce research in a domain when demand for upstream scientific research in that domain increases. In particular, I examine how scientists’ propensity to produce research in that domain varies by their research productivity and intellectual distance from the domain, and how their response patterns shape the direction of research within that domain. Empirically, I exploit an unexpected environmental policy shock—the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate—which led to an exogenous increase in demand for upstream scientific research related to electric vehicle (EV) technologies. Following the ZEV mandate, there was an increase in the number of scientists producing EV research. However, I find that as scientists’ intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists became disproportionately less likely to produce EV research than less-productive scientists. Notably, when more-productive scientists from intellectually more distant domains chose to produce EV research, they generated more novel and more impactful EV research outcomes than other scientists, including more-productive scientists from closer domains. These findings suggest a potential asymmetry in how academic scientists respond to increased demand for upstream scientific research in a domain: while more-productive scientists from intellectually more distant domains have significant potential to contribute novel and impactful research outcomes in that domain, they tend to be underrepresented among those who actually produce research in the domain.

items.title: Demystifying generative AI adoption in higher education: an integrated GRAI–AKM framework
items.abstract: Purpose Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, yet successful institutional adoption requires effective knowledge governance, organizational readiness and coordinated decision-making. Existing studies have predominantly relied on individual-level technology acceptance models, providing limited insight into organizational and knowledge management capabilities for sustainable implementation. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was employed using open-ended written responses from 20 academic professionals recruited through Prolific. The qualitative responses were analyzed using thematic analysis, and the resulting themes were mapped onto the proposed graphs with results and actions interconnected (GRAI) and active knowledge models (AKM) framework (GRAI–AKM). Findings Six themes were identified: (1) professional training and AI literacy, (2) ethical governance and academic integrity, (3) structural capital flexibility and knowledge processes, (4) trust, transparency and relational capital, (5) platform maturity and technological infrastructure and (6) human–AI complementarity. Professional training and AI literacy emerged as the most-discussed themes. The findings suggest that Gen AI adoption depends on the interaction of human, structural, technological, and knowledge resources rather than technology acceptance alone. Research limitations/implications Although based on a qualitative sample and self-reported written responses, the study advances knowledge management research by integrating Intellectual Capital (IC) and the Knowledge-Based View (KBV) into a comprehensive framework. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of AI literacy, ethical governance, organizational learning and human–AI collaboration for sustainable adoption of Gen AI in higher education. Originality/value The study provides qualitative empirical support for the GRAI–AKM framework, offering a multidimensional perspective on knowledge management for sustainable adoption of Gen AI.

items.title: Dentists’ acceptance of artificial intelligence-assisted decision support for oral potentially malignant disorder detection: a structural equation modeling study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) may support early detection and clinical decision-making of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), but clinical implementation depends on dentists’ acceptance of AI-assisted clinical decision support. This study aimed to identify structural associations of AI acceptance among dentists using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 500 dentists. Construct validity and reliability were assessed using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypothesized associations were evaluated using structural equation modeling with bootstrap mediation analysis. The extended TAM showed generally satisfactory measurement properties and good overall model fit. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention (β = 0.550), followed by AI-assisted clinical decision reliance (β = 0.220), perceived usefulness (β = 0.180), trust (β = 0.140), and perceived ease of use (β = 0.120). Significant indirect effects operated through attitude toward AI. The model explained 67.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Dentists reported favorable behavioral intention toward AI-assisted decision support for OPMD detection. Attitude toward AI showed the strongest association with behavioral intention. The findings are consistent with the extended TAM. Successful implementation will require explainable systems, clinician education, trust-building, and effective workflow integration. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations translate into actual clinical adoption. Understanding factors associated with dentists’ acceptance of AI may support the responsible integration of AI-assisted decision support into oral cancer screening pathways.

items.title: Design and Development of A Hybrid AI Chatbot for Improving Administrative Support in Educational Institutions
items.abstract: Educational institutions receive many administrative queries related to admissions, fee structures, scholarships, examinations, timetables, and required documents. Answering these queries manually can increase the workload of administrative staff and cause delays for students. This paper proposes a hybrid artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot designed to improve administrative support in educational institutions. The proposed system combines rule-based responses, information retrieval, and generative AI to handle different types of student queries. It aims to provide answers based on verified institutional documents, support common queries in English and selected Indian languages, and identify questions that require human assistance. A confidence-based response mechanism is proposed to reduce incorrect or unsupported answers. The system will be evaluated using response accuracy, response time, query-handling performance, and user feedback. The proposed approach aims to make administrative information more accessible, consistent, and efficient while reducing repetitive work for college staff.

items.title: Design and Development of an AI-Based Voice-Controlled Robot for Intelligent Human-Robot Interaction
items.abstract: Most low-cost voice-controlled robots accept only a handful of fixed words such as “forward” and “stop”, and depend on a smartphone app for speech recognition. This paper presents the design and development of an AI-based voice-controlled mobile robot that holds natural spoken conversations and turns free-form requests into safe movements. The robot is built around an ESP32 microcontroller with an INMP441 I²S MEMS microphone, a MAX98357A I²S class-D amplifier and speaker, an L298N dual H-bridge driving two DC gear motors with wheels, a servo for head and gesture movements, and a 2S pack of 18650 lithium-ion cells with a main switch. A hybrid architecture is used: a compact keyword-spotting model on the ESP32 detects the wake word and a local “stop” command without any network, while the spoken request is streamed to an AI server where speech-to-text, a large language model and text-to-speech produce a structured JSON action and a spoken reply. A command validator on the ESP32 checks every action against a whitelist, speed limits and a time-out before the motors move, so the language model can never drive the robot outside its safe envelope. A review of 19 related studies shows that earlier robots offered either fixed-vocabulary control on cheap hardware or natural-language interaction on expensive platforms, but rarely both. Design calculations show that a 4-second request needs 128 kB of audio, well within the ESP32's memory, and that the battery pack supports an estimated 13.4 h of mixed use. An experimental protocol with metrics for recognition accuracy, latency, safety response and user experience is provided for prototype validation.

items.title: Design and preliminary validation of an AI enhanced game based learning environment for computational thinking in upper secondary education
items.abstract: Abstract Integrating generative artificial intelligence within game-based learning offers promising but still-maturing possibilities for computational thinking (CT) education. This developmental research study (Type I) reports the design and preliminary validation of an AI-enhanced game-based learning environment (AI-GBLE) for upper-secondary students. Grounded in constructivism, cognitive load theory, information processing theory, mental models theory, and game-based learning principles, the environment integrates six components on the Roblox platform—problem-based scenarios, learning resources, collaborative learning, a CT enhancement centre, scaffolding, and an AI coaching system combining a GPT-4-powered conversational non-player character with a rule-based adaptive difficulty engine—within an authentic Smart Greenhouse (Internet of Things) context. Following expert appraisal of content, instructional design, and media-technology quality by nine specialists, three per domain, 30 Grade 11 students in Thailand used the environment across eight 60-minute sessions over six weeks in a one-group pretest–posttest validation. Students showed pre–post gains of 3.07 points on the 20-point computational thinking test (Wilcoxon r = .86; Cohen’s d_av = 2.79) and 5.90 points on the 15-point achievement test (d_av = 3.23)—standardised effects inflated by ceiling compression—and reported strong immediate satisfaction across six acceptance dimensions (overall M = 4.64). Because the single-group design precludes causal attribution, these findings are interpreted as preliminary evidence—of feasibility, acceptability, and learning-related signals from a developed prototype—rather than as intervention effectiveness. The individual contributions of the AI coach, adaptive engine, and other components were not empirically established. The study contributes a theory-mapped design heuristic for AI-augmented game-based learning and identifies controlled comparisons, improved measurement, and mechanism-focused analyses as priorities for subsequent research.

items.title: Development and validation of an AI approach for hyperbilirubinemia assessment from routine haematology in high-altitude settings
items.abstract: Background: Hypobaric hypoxia at extreme altitudes induces compensatory erythropoiesis, alters bilirubin metabolism, and increases the risk of high-altitude hyperbilirubinemia (HBIL). Conventional serum bilirubin screening in these regions is frequently constrained by limited medical infrastructure. This study aims to develop a machine learning pipeline that uses universally accessible routine haematological parameters to infer serum bilirubin status and stratify disease severity. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of permanent high-altitude residents (>2,900 m) to develop and validate diagnostic models using routine haematological parameters. We employed a Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network for primary diagnosis and clinical severity stratification (latent vs. overt jaundice). We evaluated model performance using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and validated the approach in an independent temporal hold-out validation cohort. We interpreted feature importance using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results: The model exhibited strong discriminative capacity, achieving an AUROC of 0.918 for primary diagnosis and 0.888 for disease severity stratification in the internal validation set. It maintained predictive efficacy in the temporal hold-out validation cohort, with AUROC values of 0.923 and 0.905, respectively. Interpretability analysis revealed that the magnitude of compensatory erythrocytosis (Hb and Hct) was primarily associated with the initial onset of HBIL. Furthermore, erythrocyte morphological heterogeneity (RDW-SD) distinguished the transition to overt jaundice. Conclusions: This study establishes a scalable, artificial intelligence-driven framework for screening and risk-stratifying high-altitude HBIL using routine blood parameters. This approach provides a practical, low-cost strategy for proactive clinical management in resource-constrained extreme environments.

items.title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence for Parkinson’s Disease Detection Using Handwriting and Drawing Tasks: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the performance of deep learning (DL)-based methods for classifying individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD) from handwriting and drawing tasks, following PRISMA guidelines. Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, and Science.gov were searched from 1 July to 17 July 2026, without publication date restrictions. Eligible studies evaluated a DL architecture for PD detection using handwriting or drawing and reported at least one of five performance metrics: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, or F1-score. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using PROBAST+AI. Performance estimates were logit-transformed and pooled separately using random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q, I2, and τ2, and results were presented using forest plots with 95% confidence intervals. Potential sources of heterogeneity were investigated through subgroup analyses according to DL architecture, dataset, task, and validation procedure, together with sensitivity analyses. Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Of 5233 unique records identified, 30 studies were included. Overall pooled performance exceeded 92% across the evaluated metrics. No significant differences were found between fully DL and hybrid approaches or among DL algorithms. Dataset-related differences were observed but were inconsistent across performance metrics. Combined handwriting and drawing tasks consistently achieved higher performance (>95%) than individual tasks, while cross-validation was associated with higher accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity than hold-out validation. Despite these promising findings, substantial heterogeneity and very low certainty of evidence limit the current clinical applicability of these approaches. More standardized protocols, subject-level data separation, and external validation in independent populations are needed to develop robust and generalizable AI models and clarify the potential of handwriting and drawing as non-invasive tools for PD detection.

items.title: Digital affective literacy and algorithmic mediation in the reconfiguration of educational relationships in higher education
items.abstract: Generative AI is reconfiguring educational relationships in higher education, entering university study in the passages where doubt, error, and the need for feedback emerge. The pedagogical question concerns the quality of the training experience when artificial responses become ordinary learning practices. The article presents digital affective literacy as a necessary skill for engaging with AI ethically, through critical judgment and responsibility, in continuity with developments in AI literacy and its affective domain (Cuomo, Biagini, & Ranieri, 2022; Pretorius & Cahusac de Caux, 2024). The theoretical framework integrates AI in education, AI literacy, ethics of educational technologies, pedagogical care, teacher reflexivity, flipped learning, and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). The literature recognises the potential of AI for personalisation, accessibility, and study support, while recalling the role of educational mediation in preserving students' judgment (UNESCO, 2023). items.title: Digital affective literacy and artificial intelligence in lower secondary school.
items.abstract: The introduction of generative artificial intelligence into school environments cannot be interpreted as a mere expansion of the educational toolkit. It affects the very architecture of the educational experience, altering the coordinates through which epistemic authority, relationships, and pedagogical mediation are understood. If, as Floridi (2014) argues, the contemporary condition is characterized by a progressive integration between online and offline, the school can no longer be conceived as a physical environment assisted by technologies, but rather as a node within the infosphere where the human and the artificial permanently cohabit. Conversational systems based on large language models occupy a peculiar position in this scenario. Unlike previous educational technologies, they do not limit themselves to providing content or structuring exercises; instead, they produce dialogic, contextualized, and adaptive language. This linguistic performativity allows them to be perceived as interlocutors rather than mere tools. items.abstract: Physical Education (PE) represents an emotionally rich learning environment where students experience continuous interactions, feedback loops, and embodied activities that strongly shape motivation, self-efficacy, and social participation. In recent years, this context has been increasingly influenced by digital technologies and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) systems. International evidence indicates that the combination of digital tools and social-emotional learning (SEL) pathways can significantly enhance students' outcomes in PE, supporting motivation, engagement, and inclusive participation (Saqinah et al., 2025). At the same time, a recent scoping review of 63 studies highlights that SEL development in PE remains theoretically fragmented and only partially aligned with the main pedagogical models adopted in the field (Dyson et al., 2021). This gap suggests the need for frameworks capable of integrating emotional, relational, and technological dimensions in a coherent and ethically grounded manner. items.title: Digital Competence Development Among University Lecturers: A Bibliometric Mapping of Research Trends (2010–2026)
items.abstract: The new requirements arising from digital transformation and generative artificial intelligence necessitate a reassessment of state-of-the-art research in digital competence. This bibliometric review synthesised literature on the topic of digital competence development among university lecturers, published from 2010 to May 2026. A total of 159 publications were included from an initial 746 records retrieved from the Scopus database. The search was conducted on 17 May 2026 using keyword combinations related to digital competence, competence development, academic staff, and higher education. Deduplication of search results, followed by title and abstract screening by two independent researchers, resulted in the exclusion of irrelevant records from further consideration. Performance analysis and science mapping were conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Publications increased from 18 in 2023 to 60 in 2025. The corpus received a total of 1826 citations, with an average of 11.48 citations per publication. The most cited article addressed educators’ preparedness for generative artificial intelligence (AI) (230 citations). Spain led publication output with 23 publications, followed by China with 19 and Indonesia with 12. The largest collaboration component connected 34 countries and territories. The author–keyword network comprised 88 keywords distributed across 5 clusters. Thematic mapping identified three basic clusters concerning competence, professional development, and technology-supported teaching and access. Across the three periods analysed, higher education and digital literacy remained persistent themes, while related topics evolved over time. These findings emphasise the need to embed professional learning within institutional strategies to connect individual capabilities, pedagogical practice, and responsible AI use. Future research should evaluate these connections through observed teaching practices and learner outcomes.

items.title: Digital financial literacy and trust in hybrid AI advisory: Explaining perceived private wealth management capability among digitally engaged retail investors in an emerging market
items.abstract: This study investigates how digital financial literacy, perceived transparency of artificial intelligence advisory services, investment and wealth knowledge, and cyber-risk self-protection shape Perceived Private Wealth Management Capability (PWMC) among digitally engaged retail investors in an emerging-market context. PWMC is conceptualized as a self-assessed capability outcome rather than an objective indicator of wealth-management performance, portfolio returns, or private-banking status. Drawing on the financial capability framework, trust in automation theory, and protection motivation theory, the study develops a trust-to-capability model in which trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory and digital wealth management behavior serves as a key explanatory mechanism. A non-probability sample of 249 digitally engaged retail investors in Vietnam was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling in SmartPLS 4.1, with 5,000 bootstrap subsamples. The results show that digital financial literacy is the strongest antecedent of trust in hybrid artificial intelligence advisory (β = 0.517, p < 0.001). At the same time, perceived advisory transparency also exerts a significant positive effect (β = 0.261, p < 0.001). Investment and wealth knowledge emerged as the strongest predictor of digital wealth management behavior (β = 0.348, p < 0.001). Trust, digital wealth management behavior, and investment and wealth knowledge each positively influence perceived private wealth management capability. Digital wealth management behavior partially mediates the effects of trust, investment, and wealth knowledge on perceived capability. Cyber-risk self-protection limited evidence of a boundary condition by strengthening the relationship between trust and digital wealth management behavior. However, the effect size is small and should be interpreted cautiously (β = 0.098, p = 0.038). The model explains 60.2% of the variance in digital wealth management behavior and 44.3% of the variance in perceived private wealth management capability. By moving beyond conventional explanations of robo-advisory adoption and technology acceptance, this study theorizes hybrid AI advisory as a calibrated trust environment in which retail investors’ perceived capability depends not only on whether they trust AI-supported advice but also on whether that trust translates into protective, enacted digital wealth management behavior. The findings should be interpreted in the context of digitally engaged retail investors. They should not be generalized to private banking clients, high-net-worth investors, objective portfolio performance, or verified wealth outcomes.

items.title: DIGITAL HUMAN RIGHTS: PRIVACY OF PERSONAL DATA AND THREATS IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: This article examines the evolving landscape of digital human rights, with particular focus on personal data privacy and the emerging threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on international legal frameworks — including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — the article analyses the gap between existing legal protections and the rapidly advancing digital ecosystem. Through doctrinal legal analysis and a comparative case study methodology, the research identifies key vulnerabilities in current data protection regimes and evaluates institutional responses at the international, regional, and national levels. The findings demonstrate that while significant legal infrastructure exists, enforcement remains inconsistent and AI-specific regulation is still nascent. The article concludes with policy recommendations aimed at strengthening digital rights protection frameworks, with particular reference to Uzbekistan.

items.title: Digital Tools for Risk Assessment and Decision-Making in Business Operations
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper analyses how digital tools such as artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and digital twin technologies can enhance risk assessment and decision-making in business operations. Design/Methodology/Approach: The research studies the existing literature on digital transformation and risk management, drawing on 29 publications from 2020 to 2026 (27 journal articles published in the Scopus database and two book chapters). The publications are analysed using thematic synthesis based on three constructs: digital tools, risk assessment capability, and decision-making performance. Research Limitation: The study is based on existing literature, indicating the need for further research on the practical implementation of digital technologies in different business environments. Findings: The results suggest that introducing digital technologies into management systems speeds decision-making, improves risk management, and makes organisations more competitive. Digital technologies enable organisations to process large amounts of real-time data, detect potential risks, and support more informed, timely managerial decisions. Practical Implication: The findings show that digital tools can improve risk assessment procedures and support more effective managerial decision-making. Social Implication: More efficient decision-making and risk management contribute to greater organisational resilience in dynamic business environments. Originality/Value: The study addresses two gaps in the literature: insufficient analysis of technology combinations and the human factor. In its tool-to-capability framework, digital tools contribute to operational performance indirectly by affecting risk assessment and decision-making, an effect the synthesis links to governance and managerial competencies.

items.abstract: Digital transformation is changing the way banks and financial institutions work. It affects how they process payments, manage investments, check transactions, protect customer data and meet regulatory rules. Banks now use digital platforms, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud systems and data analytics to improve speed, accuracy and control across their operations. This change is important for international banking. A single financial transaction can involve clients, banks, payment networks, regulators and service providers in different countries. Each party must share accurate information and complete its task within the required time. Digital systems help connect these activities and reduce manual work. Mumbai is a major financial centre in India. It has domestic and international banks, investment firms, stock exchanges and financial service companies. As these organisations adopt new technology, the need for professionals who understand both finance and digital operations is also changing. Global & Investment Banking Operations in Mumbai is therefore a relevant field for people who want to build careers at the meeting point of banking, investment services and technology. The Main Drivers of Digital Transformation Several factors are pushing financial institutions to update their systems and processes. 1. Faster financial transactions Customers and businesses expect payments and transfers to move quickly. Banks must process high volumes of transactions while keeping records accurate. Digital payment platforms and automated workflows help reduce delays and manual work. 2. Stronger risk controls Banks must identify suspicious activity, prevent fraud and protect customer information. Digital monitoring systems can review large volumes of data and flag unusual activity for further checks. 3. Better customer service Digital platforms allow customers to access account information, submit documents and track requests. Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) APIs allow different software systems to exchange information. items.title: DIGITAL TWINS IN PHARMACEUTICAL AND BIOPHARMACEUTICAL MANUFACTURING: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Digital twin (DT) technology has become a significant advancement in smart manufacturing and is increasingly being adopted in pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industries under the concepts of industry 4.0 and pharma 4.0. A digital twin generates a synchronized virtual image of physical manufacturing system that continuously exchanges in real time information for process monitoring, prediction and optimization. This review discusses the architecture and framework of digital systems including physical components, virtual models, and data management platforms. It explains the functional architecture and interactive mapping of DT-based protection systems and highlight the role of supporting technologies such as Internet of Things (IoT), process analytical technology (PAT), cloud computing, machine learning, and manufacturing execution systems. Using digital twins in pharmaceutical production for process design, quality control, predictive maintenance, material tracking and continuous manufacturing is also presented. different modelling approaches including mechanistic, data driven, and hybrid models are discussed along with their significance in process optimization and decision making. Furthermore, the review investigates the application of digital twin technology in biopharmaceutical production as well as its ability to raise product quality and production efficiency. challenges associated with implementation such as data security commerce system integration computational requirements and regulatory compliance are also addressed. finally further development including artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (MI), edge computing, blockchain technology and cloud-based DT systems are highlighted. digital twin technology offers significant opportunities for improving pharmaceutical manufacturing efficacy reliability and product quality, making it a potentially useful tool for smart manufacturing systems of the future.

items.abstract: Abstract Irrigation water is a recognized pathway for pre-harvest contamination of fresh produce, yet conventional laboratory testing limits monitoring frequency and timeliness of management decisions. This critical review examines how digital technologies - Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors, rapid biosensors and molecular methods, and artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning - may support irrigation water monitoring and pre-harvest food safety. Literature was purposively selected from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink and IEEE Xplore, with an initial scoping from January 2018 to October 2026; the final 29 peer-reviewed studies that met critical relevance criteria clustered between 2020 and 2026, including two 2026 early-online articles, reflecting the recent emergence of this field. The review was complemented by guidance from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Codex Alimentarius Commission (2023), World Health Organization (WHO) and United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA 2024 Final Rule on Pre-Harvest Agricultural Water). The synthesis shows that IoT systems can increase monitoring frequency for physicochemical parameters and support baseline characterization and anomaly detection, while rapid biosensors and molecular assays offer more direct detection of microbial hazards with reduced time-to-result compared with conventional culture. AI approaches can assist pattern recognition, risk prediction and interpretation of multi-parameter data. However, physicochemical measurements cannot independently confirm microbiological safety, and sensor accuracy, calibration drift, matrix interference, field validation and model transferability remain critical limitations. Integrated digital monitoring may support risk-based water management when combined with validated microbial testing and clear response procedures, but evidence that it directly reduces produce contamination under routine farming conditions remains limited. Recommendations are provided for strengthening field validation and implementation, particularly in resource-limited locations.

items.title: Does generative AI improve university students’ independent English language proficiency?
items.abstract: The growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education raises important questions about its contribution to students’ independent learning outcomes. This study examines whether structured AI-assisted learning improves university students’ independent English language proficiency compared with unrestricted AI use and conventional instruction. A quantitative, quasi-experimental design is proposed involving 150 undergraduate and postgraduate students assigned to three instructional groups. English proficiency is assessed through pre-tests, post-tests, and delayed tests conducted without AI assistance, covering grammar, vocabulary, academic writing, reading comprehension, and speaking. Regression analysis is proposed to examine the roles of instructional approach, self-regulated learning, prior AI experience, baseline proficiency, and age in explaining proficiency gains. The study seeks to distinguish AI-supported task performance from independently demonstrated language competence and retained learning. Its anticipated contribution is to inform evidence-based integration of GenAI into university language education, emphasising structured use, learner autonomy, and independent assessment.

items.title: Domain Adaptation for Cross-Project Defect Prediction via Transfer-Contrastive Learning with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) is a significant solution in software defect prediction (SDP) when historical data is unavailable. In CPDP, the defect data of another project (called the source project) is used to train the model. Different training and test projects may have different feature distributions. Divergence in data distribution between source and target projects adversely affects prediction performance, and the semantic information of the tokens cannot be captured adequately. However, most of the existing deep learning approaches assume that these two projects have a uniform distribution, so the features extracted from these deep learning models are not optimal. Moreover, these approaches neglected the information about the class to which the sample belonged and were unable to discriminate the samples according to the class information. To address this issue, we proposed a framework, TC3, that exploits the combination of contrastive and transfer learning integrated with the CNN-CodeBERT model to learn class-discriminative information and obtain more transferable features for the target project. The proposed model was evaluated on PROMISE datasets. The proposed model achieved an absolute F1-score improvement of 0.047 to 0.107, corresponding to a relative improvement of 7.89% to 19.96%, and an absolute AUC improvement of 0.014 to 0.148, corresponding to a relative improvement of 2.18% to 29.19% as compared to the baseline methods.

items.title: Domain Knowledge Plus AI Fluency: The New Nonnegotiable Competency for the Health Workforce in the AI Era
items.abstract: In the ongoing AI boom—now supercharged by large language models and generative AI tools—the rapid integration of AI into health care and public health has created an urgent need for professionals who combine deep domain expertise (clinical, epidemiological, ethical, and contextual expertise in health and public health) with AI fluency (the ability to understand, critically evaluate, use, and oversee AI systems effectively). Without domain guidance, AI risks producing biased, unsafe, or contextually irrelevant outputs that compromise patient safety and exacerbate disparities. Conversely, domain experts lacking AI fluency may underuse or misuse these technologies, missing opportunities to improve care quality, operational efficiency, and population health. A foundational understanding of the modern AI system stack—comprising energy, accelerators, infrastructure, models, and applications—empowers health professionals to make informed decisions on adoption, evaluation, governance, and ethical use without needing to code or build models themselves. This stack framework highlights critical interdependencies and health care–specific challenges, including regulatory compliance, data privacy, sustainability, and resource constraints, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This paper argues that cultivating domain-AI bilingualism is essential for safe, effective, and equitable AI integration worldwide. It outlines the 5-layer AI system stack applied to health care, key reasons for hybrid expertise, and a practical 4-step pathway: awakening (recognizing AI’s transformative role), intrepidity (courageously engaging foundational AI concepts), bilingualism (translating between clinical needs and AI capabilities), and visionary leadership (driving organizational and policy readiness). It outlines major barriers, targeted strategies, and recommendations for educators, institutions, and policymakers. By bridging domain knowledge with AI fluency, health professionals can direct—rather than be directed by—AI technologies, including emerging agentic systems, toward more precise, sustainable, and human-centered outcomes while mitigating risks. This hybrid capability represents a nonnegotiable competency for the health workforce for thriving in the post-2026 AI era.

items.title: Dual-wheel Drive and Collaborative Education: AI-empowered Innovation and Entrepreneurship Education for Emerging Engineering
items.abstract: In response to practical problems in innovation and entrepreneurship education for emerging engineering in local application-oriented universities — including weak industrial alignment, limited practice scenarios, and insufficient integration of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy — this paper focuses on mechanical and electrical majors and develops a dual-wheel education framework: the endogenous drive of theoretical and practical teaching, the exogenous drive of industrial demand and skills competitions. It integrates AI technology throughout teaching, practice and evaluation, and establishes a school-enterprise-government collaborative education mechanism. In line with the development needs of Quanzhou’s intelligent manufacturing industry, teaching reforms are implemented across four dimensions: curriculum system optimisation, practice platform construction, teaching staff development and evaluation mechanism improvement. Taking mechanical and electrical majors at Quanzhou University of Information Engineering as the pilot, this study adopts an action research approach and evaluates implementation effects through questionnaire surveys, practical performance assessment and competition outcome analysis. The pilot findings suggest that this model may improve students’ engineering practical skills and innovation and entrepreneurship literacy, and offers a potential practical approach for emerging engineering education reform in local application-oriented universities.

items.title: Dynamic PGA: A Human-Centered Framework for Continuously Adaptive AI Experiences
items.abstract: Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) is a human-centered conceptual framework for continuously adaptive AI experiences. The framework explores how artificial intelligence might adapt not only to an individual's longer-range goals, interests, knowledge, and preferences, but also to meaningful changes that occur as an experience unfolds. The paper introduces a developing Dynamic A/B model: Dynamic A provides adaptive direction around the individual's goals and intended destination, while Dynamic B introduces state-aware responsiveness to the individual's immediate circumstances. Together, they express a central principle of the framework: A remembers the destination. B respects the human being who has to get there. Version 1.0 explores potential applications in education, experiential travel, professional environments, healthcare communication, and creative work, while emphasizing human agency, privacy, appropriate boundaries, and future research and validation.
